title: Neurotechnology-enabled motor Recovery via Individualized Selective EMG biomarkers
summary:
Background:
Recovery and therapy outcomes after stroke can differ greatly between patients. Especially in people with severe paralysis, it is often unclear why some individuals respond well to rehabilitation training while others do not. Conventional studies usually compare average effects across large groups of patients and may therefore overlook important individual improvements. The aim of this study is to investigate the recovery process of each participant as precisely as possible.

Research Question:
The study investigates whether individuals with severe paralysis after stroke still show residual motor capacities years after the event and whether these can become detectable again through training with a brain-controlled hand exoskeleton. The study further examines whether early signs of voluntary muscle activity can be detected before visible improvements in motor function occur. In addition, we aim to better understand why some patients respond more strongly or more rapidly to the training than others. In particular, we are interested in the role of damage to specific brain regions and neural pathways, as well as the severity of the initial impairment, in influencing treatment response.


Methods:
In this study, four patients with chronic stroke will train with a brain-controlled hand exoskeleton over a period of 8 weeks. The system supports hand movements by using signals from the nervous system. During the training sessions, patients perform everyday-like movements with the assistance of the hand exoskeleton.
conditions: Chronic stroke patients (Stroke onset more than 12 months ago)

interventions.name:
Intervention: Brain/Neural-controlled hand exoskeleton training of bimanual tasks for neurorehabilitation after stroke
